position_phrase: a Career Development Research Fellow in Economics
fit_paragraph: A four-year fellowship at St John's would give my research the time its next steps need: taking the two-step design of the Phillips curve paper from sectors to firms, and asking what debt issuance does to convenience yields outside the euro area. Oxford's Department of Economics has one of the strongest monetary groups in Europe, and the work of Andrea Ferrero and Martin Ellison on monetary policy and public debt is close to both projects. I would also welcome the College's tutorial teaching: I have taught small groups online for three years and would be glad to do it in person.

St. Gallen is a natural fit for my research. Winfried Koeniger's work on consumption, household finance and labor markets and Reto Föllmi's on international macroeconomics sit close to my two strands, and the department's empirical orientation is how I like to work. I also know Switzerland well: my master's is from Geneva, my Ph.D. from Bern, and my collaborators at the BIS are an hour away in Basel. I can teach macroeconomics at every level in English and French.

position_phrase: a Junior Economist in the Economics Department
fit_paragraph: The Economics Department works on the questions in my job market paper: the post-pandemic inflation surge, labor shortages and how much of each country's experience is shared across the OECD. My paper uses the European Commission's business surveys, the same kind of business tendency data the OECD compiles for its members, and the two-step design extends naturally to the cross-country analysis in the Economic Outlook and the country surveys. My time at the BIS and the ESM taught me to write for policymakers under deadline, and I would be glad to do so again in Paris.

Kellogg's finance group is where my work on safe assets would grow best. Konstantin Milbradt's research on safe asset determination and Sergio Rebelo's on international finance and inflation span the two strands of my own, and Northwestern's macroeconomists are close at hand. I would bring a European complement to the group's work on Treasury markets: the euro area has several safe issuers in one currency, a setting in which spillovers between convenience yields can be measured directly.

position_phrase: an Assistant Professor of International Macroeconomics
fit_paragraph: International macroeconomics is where the two strands of my research meet. The Phillips curve paper asks how much of a country's inflation comes from shocks shared across the euro area, and the convenience yield paper measures how one country's debt issuance moves another's borrowing costs. Sarah Zubairy's work on fiscal and monetary policy and Tatevik Sekhposyan's on the identification of monetary policy shocks are close to my own, and I would be glad to teach international macroeconomics at the undergraduate and graduate level.
